entries.narration: Python is a general-purpose programming language, and before we write a single line of it, it is worth knowing what kind of language it is, because those five words on the left of the screen explain almost everything you will meet in this course. It is high-level: you describe what you want done, and Python takes care of how the machine does it, so you never manage memory addresses or registers. It is interpreted: you write a file and run it, with no separate compile step to wait for, which is why trying an idea in Python takes seconds. It is dynamically typed: a value knows its own type, a number or a piece of text, but a name does not, so the same name can point at different kinds of value over time. It is garbage-collected: when nothing uses a value any more, Python reclaims the memory for you. And it is multi-paradigm: you can write a ten-line script, a set of small functions, or a system built from objects, and all three are ordinary Python. Now look to the right. The same language turns up in very different jobs. Web sites and the services behind them, with Django, Flask and FastAPI. Data analysis in notebooks, with pandas, NumPy and Jupyter. Machine learning, where PyTorch, TensorFlow and scikit-learn are written to be driven from Python. Data engineering, where Airflow schedules pipelines, PySpark drives Spark, and DuckDB queries files directly. Infrastructure tools like Ansible, the cloud providers' own SDKs, and countless command-line tools. And the everyday automation of moving files, filling spreadsheets and reading web pages. This course stays in one of these worlds, data engineering, and builds a real pipeline from an empty folder. But everything you learn transfers to the others, because it is all the same language. Next, where that language came from.

Python is older than most people expect. In December 1989, Guido van Rossum, a programmer at the CWI research institute in Amsterdam, started writing a new language over the holidays. He had a specific gap in mind. Guido had worked on ABC, a language designed to be easy to read and teach, but ABC was closed: you could not extend it or connect it to the outside world. And on Amoeba, the operating system project he was working on, he kept needing something in between the two tools he had. Shell scripts were quick to write but too weak for real programs. C was powerful, but slow to write and to debug. Python was built to sit in that gap: as readable as ABC, but open, extensible, and able to talk to the operating system. He named it after the comedy series Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake. The first public version, 0.9.0, appeared in February 1991, and it already had classes, exceptions, functions, and the lists, dictionaries and strings you will use in almost every program in this course. Version 1.0 followed in January 1994. The second era began in October 2000 with Python 2.0, which brought list comprehensions, a compact way of building lists that you will meet in the processing course, and a garbage collector that could clean up objects referring to each other. In 2001 the Python Software Foundation was formed to own the language, so it no longer depended on one company or one person. Then, in December 2008, came the decision that defines modern Python. Python 3.0 deliberately broke compatibility with Python 2, to fix mistakes that could not be fixed any other way. The table on the right shows the ones you would notice. Print became a function. Dividing seven by two gives three and a half instead of quietly throwing away the half. Text became Unicode by default, so names in any language just work. The two versions lived side by side for over a decade, until Python 2 reached its end of life in January 2020. Since then, Python 3 has moved quickly. Guido stepped down as the language's lead in 2018, and an elected Steering Council took over. Since 2020 a new version has shipped every October. Python 3.11 made the interpreter about twenty five percent faster on average. Python 3.13 added an experimental build without the global interpreter lock, and 3.14 made that build officially supported. That lock, and what removing it means, is part of the next course.

Most languages have a style guide. Python has a philosophy, and it ships inside the language. Type python, dash m, this, and Python prints nineteen short lines called the Zen of Python, written by Tim Peters, one of the language's early core developers. The terminal picks out three of them. You do not need to memorise the rest, but three ideas run through all of them, and they will shape every piece of code in this course. The first is that readability counts. Code is read far more often than it is written, so Python is designed to be read. Look at the small file in the editor. There are no braces and no end markers. The indentation itself is the structure: the line that prints is indented under the if, which is indented under the for, and that is exactly how Python runs it: the terminal shows the two big orders, and nothing for the small one. What you see is what runs. The second idea is batteries included. Python ships with a large standard library, so a lot of real work needs nothing installed at all. The modules on the right are the ones our pipeline will use: csv and json to read the shop's files, sqlite3 to load a database, pathlib to find files, datetime for dates, decimal for money, statistics for summaries, and logging to record what happened. The last one, timeit, measures speed, and the next section uses it. Every one of them comes with Python. The third idea is in the line about having one obvious way to do it, and in how the language changes. Every change to Python is written up as a PEP, a Python Enhancement Proposal, discussed in public, and accepted or rejected by the elected Steering Council. Beyond the standard library, the Python Package Index holds hundreds of thousands of packages written by the community. In this course we stay with the standard library for the pipeline itself, and add a few tools only when we start testing and checking it. Next, an honest look at what Python is good at, and what it is not.

No language is the right choice for everything, and knowing where Python fits will make you a better engineer than pretending it fits everywhere. The table on the right is the honest version. Python is strong for automation and for gluing systems together, because the code is short and the standard library covers so much. It is strong for data analysis and machine learning. It is strong for data pipelines, which is what we are building. For web back ends it is good, and frameworks like Django and FastAPI run large sites, though at very large scale teams sometimes reach for Go or Java. And it is a weak choice for mobile apps, and not a native choice in the browser, where Kotlin, Swift and JavaScript own the platforms. The interesting row is the slow one, and the file in the editor shows why. It adds up the same million numbers two ways. The function loop sum does it with an ordinary Python loop, one number at a time. The other calls the built-in sum function. The first line of output checks that both give exactly the same answer, and then timeit, from the standard library, runs each one many times and keeps the best. On the machine this course was made on, the loop took a little over twenty milliseconds, and sum under five: between four and five times faster, for exactly the same answer. The numbers will differ on your machine, but the gap will not go away, and the reason is worth understanding now. A Python loop runs one bytecode instruction at a time, with the interpreter checking types as it goes. The built-in sum does the same work in compiled C. That is also the secret behind Python's strength in data and machine learning: NumPy, pandas and PyTorch keep their inner loops in C, C plus plus or on a GPU, and Python only directs them. So the rule is simple. Write the logic in Python, and let the heavy loops run in code that was built for speed. You will see that rule again when we make the pipeline fast. Next, the pipeline itself.

Everything in this course builds one real program: a data pipeline for a small coffee roastery. Every day, the roastery's online shop writes a file of the day's orders. On the left is one of those files, as it really looks. Each line is one order: an order number, the date, the customer, the product code, and how many bags. Look at the highlighted line. The quantity says three, written as a word, not a number. Real data always has lines like that, and a good pipeline has to deal with them without crashing and without quietly getting the totals wrong. The pipeline works in three stages, and data engineers call them E, T and L. Extract reads every day's file and checks every row, keeping the good ones and reporting the bad. Transform prices each line from the product catalogue and adds up the revenue for each product. Load writes the results somewhere useful: a SQLite database that keeps every priced line, and a daily report. On the right is the report this exact file produces, from a real run. Three bags of the Ethiopian coffee, one of the Brazilian, one of the Colombian, seventy one dollars and fifty cents in total, and one order rejected, with the reason, so somebody can fix it. The small numbers on each stage are the courses that build it. Extract is course six. Transform is courses five and seven. Load is course eight. And the courses along the bottom are the ones around the pipeline: how Python runs, setting up the project, holding the data in memory, and then, once the pipeline works, structuring it, testing it, making it fast and shipping it as a job that runs on a schedule. From course three onwards, every lesson shows you the project the way a developer sees it, with the files on the left, the code in the middle, and the terminal showing exactly what happens when it runs. Next course: what actually happens when you run a Python file.

When you type python and the name of a file, it feels as if Python simply reads your code and does it. In fact your code goes through six stages before anything appears on the screen, and this frame follows one line, total equals price times quantity, through all of them. First, Python reads the file. To Python it is only text at this point. Second, the tokenizer splits that text into words, which Python calls tokens. The terminal runs the real tokenizer on the file, and shows line three becoming five tokens, a name, an equals sign, another name, a star, and a third name, followed by a marker for the end of the line. Third, the parser checks that those tokens form valid Python, and builds a tree describing what the line means: an assignment, whose value is a multiplication, whose left side is the name price and whose right side is the name quantity. If you ever get a SyntaxError, this is the stage that raised it, before a single line of your program ran. Fourth, the compiler turns the tree into bytecode: small, simple instructions for a machine that does not physically exist. The table on the right lists the four instructions this line becomes: load price, load quantity, multiply, store the result as total. Fifth, the Python virtual machine runs those instructions in a loop: fetch the next one, do it, repeat. And sixth, the result you asked for appears: nineteen point zero, the first line of output in the terminal. Two things are worth holding on to. Python is not running your text directly; it runs bytecode compiled from it, every time. And the machine that runs it is a program too, written in C, called CPython, which is the Python you installed. The rest of this course opens each stage up. Next, the bytecode itself, and where Python keeps it.

Compiling every file on every run would waste time, so Python keeps the bytecode it compiles for modules you import. Look at the project on the left. Main dot py imports a function from pricing dot py. After one run, a new folder has appeared: double underscore pycache. Inside it is pricing dot cpython three fourteen dot pyc, the compiled bytecode of the pricing module. The name tells you which interpreter made it, so if you run the same project with a different Python version, each version keeps its own cache instead of reading the wrong one. The terminal shows what that file holds for the line total function, using the dis module, Python's disassembler. Four instructions: resume, load both arguments, multiply, and return. Notice that main dot py has no pyc file. The script you run directly is compiled fresh every time and never cached; only modules you import are. The rules are short, and they are in the list on the right. An imported module is compiled once and the bytecode is saved. The cache records the source file's modification time and size, so the next time you import it, Python checks whether the source has changed: if it has, it compiles again; if not, it loads the saved bytecode and skips the work. You never need to manage this folder yourself, and it is safe to delete, because Python rebuilds it. It also belongs in your gitignore file, since it is generated, not written. In a small project you will not notice the time saved. In a large one, with hundreds of modules imported at start-up, the cache is the difference between starting instantly and starting slowly. Next, what the virtual machine does with those instructions.

Python's virtual machine is a stack machine, and once you see what that means, bytecode stops looking mysterious. Picture a stack of plates. You can put a plate on top, and you can take the top plate off, and that is all. The machine keeps a stack like that for values, and almost every instruction either pushes something onto it, or pops something off it, or both. The terminal shows the four instructions that line three becomes, and the table on the right follows them, step by step. Step one, load name price: Python looks up the name price, finds nine point five, and pushes it. The stack now holds one value. Step two, load name quantity: two goes on top, so the stack holds nine point five and two. Step three, binary op multiply: it pops the top two values, multiplies them, and pushes the single result, nineteen point zero. Step four, store name total: it pops that result and binds the name total to it, leaving the stack empty, exactly as it started. Every expression you will ever write works this way. A longer calculation simply means more loads and more operations, and the order of the instructions is the order Python evaluates your expression in, which is how operator precedence becomes real. There are no registers to manage and no addresses: everything passes through the stack, which is what makes the bytecode so compact and so easy for the interpreter to run. It is also part of why pure Python loops are slower than C: each of these small steps is a separate trip around the evaluation loop. Next, what happens to this stack when one function calls another.

A program is mostly functions calling other functions, and Python keeps track of that with a second stack, the call stack. Every time you call a function, Python creates a frame: a small record holding that function's own names and values, and the place to return to when it finishes. The new frame goes on top. When the function returns, its frame is removed, and the function underneath carries on exactly where it stopped. The file in the editor has three levels: the script itself calls order total, which calls line total. Inside line total, line seven asks Python to list the frames that exist at that moment, and the terminal shows the answer: line total, then order total, then module, which is Python's name for the script itself. Newest first. On the right is that same moment drawn as a stack. At the top, line total is running, and its frame holds just two names: the product code and the quantity. Underneath, order total is paused, waiting for line total to return. Its frame has its own names, including total, which is still zero, because the first line has not been added yet. At the bottom is the module's frame, holding the global names: the price table and the two functions. Two consequences matter for the rest of the course. Each call gets its own frame, so two functions can use the same name, like quantity, without interfering. And when something goes wrong deep inside a call, Python can tell you exactly how you got there, by reading this stack from top to bottom. That is what a traceback is, and we will read one at the end of this course. Next, what a name actually is.

Here is the most important idea in this course, and the one that surprises people coming from other languages. In Python, a variable is not a box that holds a value. It is a name, attached to an object. Look at the second line of the file. Same equals order. It is tempting to read that as copying the list. It does not copy anything. It takes the name same and attaches it to the object that order already refers to. There is still exactly one list. Then the third line appends a third coffee to it through the name same, and the terminal shows the result: printing order shows three items, because order and same are two names for the same list. Python confirms it two ways: same is order is true, and the two identities are equal. The diagram on the right shows the real arrangement. Names live in a namespace, which is simply a dictionary from names to objects; at the top level of a script it is called the global namespace, and every function call gets a fresh one of its own, in its frame. Objects live separately, on the heap, and a name only ever points at one. So assignment never copies. It binds a name. If you actually want a second, independent list, you have to ask for one, with a copy, and you will see how in the course on holding data. Keep this picture in mind whenever a value seems to change behind your back: the question to ask is how many names point at that object. Next, the objects themselves.

Every object in Python has exactly three things: an identity, a type, and a value, and knowing which one you are asking about prevents a whole class of bugs. In this file, a and b are two lists built separately with the same contents. The terminal shows what Python thinks of them. A equals equals b is true: double equals compares values, and both lists hold the same two products. But a is b is false: is compares identity, and these are two different objects. The third line prints their identities with the id function. In CPython the identity is the object's address in memory, which is why the numbers are large, and why you will see different numbers every time you run it. Only the comparison matters, never the number itself. The fourth line asks for types: a is a list, and len of a is an int. The type decides what an object can do; a list can be appended to, an int can be added. On the right, the two objects sit on the heap, one above the other: different identities, the same type, equal values. So the rule is simple. Use double equals to ask whether two things have the same value, which is what you want almost every time. Use is only to ask whether two names point at the very same object, and in everyday code that mostly means checking for None, as in x is None. Mixing them up is a classic bug: two lists can be equal without being the same object, and changing one then leaves the other untouched. Next, how long an object lives, and who decides when it goes.

Python reclaims memory for you, and the main way it does it is surprisingly simple. Every object keeps a count of how many references point at it. When the count drops to zero, nothing can reach the object any more, and CPython frees it immediately. This file watches the count change. Python's sys module has a function, getrefcount, that reports it, with one catch: the act of passing the object to the function adds a temporary reference, so it always reports one more than you might expect. The table on the right shows both numbers. After order is created, there is one real reference and getrefcount says two. Binding a second name, alias, makes it two real references and three reported. Deleting alias brings it back down. Del does not destroy the object, by the way. It removes a name, and the count goes down with it. Reference counting has one blind spot: a cycle. The last lines of the file build a dictionary that contains itself. When its name is deleted, the dictionary still refers to itself, so its count can never reach zero, and counting alone would keep it forever. For that, CPython has a second mechanism, the cycle collector, which periodically looks for groups of objects that only refer to each other. Calling gc dot collect runs it now, and it reports that it freed one object: our self-referencing dictionary. In practice you will almost never call it yourself; it runs automatically. What you should take away is the model: an object lives as long as something refers to it, and the pipeline we build will lean on that when it processes a month of orders without holding them all in memory. Next, the lock that has shaped Python's history.

Your computer almost certainly has several processor cores, so it is natural to expect two threads to do twice the work in the same time. Whether they do depends on which build of Python you run, and this frame runs the same file on both. The file counts down from twenty million twice, first one count after the other, then on two threads at once, using a thread pool from the standard library. The first run in the terminal is the default build, the one you get from python dot org. Both ways take under a second; run it a few times and the numbers trade places, which is just noise. Two threads gave no speed-up. The reason is the global interpreter lock, the GIL. In the default build a thread must hold this one lock to run Python bytecode, so only one thread runs bytecode at any moment, however many cores you have. The lock kept CPython's memory management simple and safe, which is why the reference counting from the last section needs no extra locks. It does not make threads useless: a thread waiting for a file, a database or the network releases the lock while it waits, so threads that mostly wait still overlap well, and the pipeline will use exactly that. Now the second run. It is the same file, run with python three fourteen t, the free-threaded build, which has no GIL. It was experimental in Python 3.13 and became officially supported in 3.14. Here the two threads finished clearly sooner, because each one ran on its own core. Not in half the time: starting threads and sharing memory safely has a cost, and on this machine it came to roughly two thirds of the time, run after run. The price is in the list: it is a separate interpreter you install on purpose, and the Python 3.14 documentation puts its cost for single-threaded code at roughly five to ten percent, so the default build is still the default. When we make the pipeline fast, we will choose between threads, processes and asyncio with both builds in mind. Next, the last piece of the picture: reading an error.

Every Python programmer spends a lot of time reading tracebacks, and most beginners read them in the wrong order. A traceback is the call stack from earlier in this course, printed at the moment something went wrong. In this file, the order contains a product code, K E N two fifty, that is not in the price table, and the terminal shows what happens. The rule is: read it from the bottom up. The last line is what went wrong. KeyError, KEN two fifty: Python looked up that key in a dictionary and it was not there. Very often that line alone tells you the fix. The line above it is where it happened: line five, in line total, the newest frame, which was running when the error was raised. Above that is who called it: line eleven, in order total. And at the top is where the whole run started: line fifteen, in the module. The highlighted lines in the editor are those same three places, and the table on the right lays out the reading order. Reading from the top first sends you to the line where the program started, which is almost never where the problem is. Two more things to notice. A plain python run also draws little carets and tildes under each line, pointing at the exact part of the expression that failed, which matters when one line does several things. Here they are switched off with dash X no debug ranges, only so the whole stack fits on screen. And nothing after the error ran: the total was never printed. Later in the course the pipeline will catch exactly this kind of error, so that one bad product code is reported instead of stopping a whole day's run. That completes the picture of how Python runs your code. In the next course, we start the project.

From this course on, every lesson looks like this, with every panel in the same place every time: the project on the left, the way your editor shows it, the code in the middle with the terminal underneath, and the lesson's key points on the right. Today the right-hand panel is a legend for reading all the lessons that follow. Before we create a single file, here is where we are going. On the left is the roastery pipeline as it will look at the end of the course, and the table explains each part and the course that builds it. At the top is a folder called dot venv, the project's own copy of Python and its packages; we create it in the next lesson. Main dot py is the script we run. In the early courses the whole pipeline lives in this one file, because that is the clearest way to learn. The data folder holds the shop's raw files, a CSV of orders for each day and a JSON catalogue of products and prices, and the out folder is where the pipeline writes its results: a daily report and a SQLite database. The pipeline folder is where the code moves once main dot py gets too big to read in one go, in course nine: a module to extract and validate the raw files, one to price and aggregate, one to load the results, one for the data models, and one for configuration. Tests holds the automated checks we add in course ten, and pyproject dot toml describes the project and its dependencies, and eventually turns the whole thing into a command you can install. You do not need to remember this map. Every lesson shows the tree as it is at that moment, with new files marked, so you always know where you are and what has changed. Next, we start from an empty folder.

Every Python project should start the same way: an empty folder, and a virtual environment inside it. The terminal at the bottom shows the whole thing, run for real. We make a folder called roastery etl and move into it. Then python dash m venv dot venv creates the virtual environment, in a folder named dot venv. The dot at the start of the name hides it in most file listings, which is the convention. Source dot venv slash bin slash activate switches this terminal over to it, and the next two commands prove it worked: which python now points inside the project, and the version is Python 3.14. On Windows the activate script lives in a folder called Scripts instead of bin, but everything else is the same. So what is a virtual environment? The list on the right says it in five lines. It is a folder with its own python and pip, its own place for installed packages, and one small configuration file, open in the editor. Look at the two highlighted lines: home says which Python it was made from, and version says which version that was. That is the whole trick. The environment does not copy Python; it points back at it, and keeps everything you install separate. Why does that matter? Because different projects need different packages, and different versions of the same package, and installing everything into one shared Python eventually breaks something. With one environment per project, each project gets exactly what it needs and nothing else. The folder is rebuilt, never shared, so it never goes into version control; Python even writes its own gitignore file inside it for that reason. Next, the first file of the pipeline.

Here is the first file of the pipeline, main dot py, marked new in the explorer. It does very little yet, and that is the point: it gives us something real to run, and a place for the pipeline to grow. The first line starts with a hash sign, which makes it a comment. Python ignores everything after a hash on a line; comments are written for the people reading the code, and this one says in a sentence what the whole program is for. That is a good habit from the very first file. The next two lines call print, a function built into Python. A function is a named piece of behaviour, and you call it by writing its name followed by brackets. Whatever you put inside the brackets is passed to it, and print writes it to the terminal. The first call passes one piece of text, in quotes. The second passes two things separated by a comma, a piece of text and the number zero, and print writes them with a space between. Notice that the number has no quotes: the quotes are what make something text. Now the terminal. With the virtual environment active, python main dot py runs the file, and the two lines appear exactly as the program wrote them. Python ran the file from top to bottom, one line at a time, which, as you saw in the last course, really means it compiled the file to bytecode and then ran that. Zero orders processed is honest for now. Over the next courses that number becomes real: first from orders written into the code, then from the shop's own files. Next, a second way to run Python, for trying things out.

Running a file is how you build a program. But when you just want to try one line, writing a file and running it is slow, and Python has something better: the REPL. The name stands for read, evaluate, print, loop, which is exactly what it does. Type python on its own, with no file name, and the terminal shows the version and a prompt of three angle brackets. Python is now waiting for you. It reads the line you type, evaluates it, prints the result, and loops back for the next one. In the terminal, we set a price, and then ask for the price times two, and the REPL prints nineteen point zero without being asked. That is the big difference from a script: in the REPL, any expression you type has its value shown automatically. In a file, nothing is shown unless you call print. Notice too that nine point five zero came back as nineteen point zero: a number like this has no memory of how many digits you typed, which is a first hint of why money needs special care, coming in the next course. The table on the right sums it up. The REPL is for trying one line: checking how something behaves, testing a guess, exploring an object. A script is for building the program, because it is saved, and the REPL forgets everything the moment you type exit. Professional developers keep both open, side by side, exactly like this: the editor for the code they are keeping, the REPL for questions. Whenever this course says try it, the REPL is the fastest way to do so. Next, what happens when the first run goes wrong.

Every programmer's first runs fail, and the skill that matters is not avoiding errors but reading them. Here is the first error you will meet, and the most common. On line three, highlighted in the editor, a bracket was opened and never closed. Running the file produces a SyntaxError, and the terminal shows how much Python tells you. It names the file and the line: line three. It prints that line, with a caret underneath, marking the bracket that was left open. And the last line says what is wrong in plain words: the bracket was never closed. Look carefully at what did not happen. Nothing was printed at all, not even the first message, although line three is the very line that was supposed to print it, and the problem is only at the end of it. That is the stage you met in the previous course. Before running anything, Python reads and parses the whole file, and a file that is not valid Python never reaches the compiler, let alone the virtual machine. A SyntaxError means the text could not be understood, so not a single line runs. The list on the right sums it up. Found by the parser. Nothing runs. The line and the caret show you where. The last line says what. And the fix here is one character: close the bracket. Editors catch most of these as you type, by colouring the rest of the file oddly or underlining the line, so a SyntaxError is usually the cheapest error you will ever fix. It is also the friendliest: Python's messages for it have become much clearer in recent versions, and they often suggest the fix. Next, an error that waits until the program is already running.

Now every bracket is fine, but on line four, highlighted, print is spelt p r n t. This is valid Python, as far as the parser is concerned: p r n t is a perfectly good name. So this time the file compiles, and the program starts running. Look at the terminal. The first line of output appears: roastery etl, starting. Line three ran, and printed, exactly as it should. Then line four runs. Python looks up the name p r n t, in the namespaces you met in the last course, finds nothing, and raises a NameError. The traceback names the file and the line, underlines the name it could not find, and, on the last line, makes a suggestion: did you mean print? Python 3 has become very good at these hints, and they are right far more often than not. The table on the right is the real lesson of this pair of errors. A SyntaxError is found by the parser, before any line runs, so nothing happens at all. A NameError is found by the running program, when it reaches the bad line, so everything before that line has already happened. Here that only means one message was printed. But think ahead to the pipeline. When it is processing a whole day of orders, a mistake that only shows up halfway through the run is far more dangerous than one that stops it at the start, because by then it may already have written half a report. That is why we will test the pipeline in course ten, and why it will check its input before it starts writing. For now, the habit is the same for both: read the last line first, then the line it points at. That completes the setup. In the next course, we start holding real data.

The pipeline has to hold data before it can do anything with it: a product code, a quantity, a price. This course is about the shapes that data can take, and it starts with the most basic idea of all, which you already met inside the interpreter: a variable is a name for an object. On line three, sku is bound to the text E T H dash two fifty. On line four, quantity is bound to the whole number two, and on line five, price to nine ninety-five. The first line of output prints all three, and the second asks each one its type: a str, an int, and a float. Notice where the type lives. It is not on the name. Nothing in the code says sku is text; the object it refers to is text, and the object carries its own type. That is what people mean when they say Python is dynamically typed. Now the important part. Line nine says bag price equals price. That does not copy nine ninety-five into a new box. It gives the same float object a second name, and line ten proves it: bag price is price prints True, one object, two names. Then line eleven sets price to ten ninety-five. Python creates a new float, and moves the name price onto it. Nothing happens to the old object, and nothing happens to bag price, which still refers to nine ninety-five. The picture on the right shows the state after line eleven: four names above, four objects below, an arrow from each name to its object. Keep this picture in mind for the rest of the course. Every value you will meet, a number, a string, a list or a whole order, is an object somewhere, and every variable is only an arrow pointing at one. Next, the numbers themselves, and why one of them cannot be trusted with money.

Python has two everyday kinds of number, and the pipeline needs to know which is which. An int is a whole number, and Python's ints are exact and have no size limit. Line eight prints two to the power of one hundred, all thirty-one digits of it, exactly. Many languages would have overflowed long before that. A float is a number with a fractional part, and it is stored the way the hardware stores it: sixty-four bits, as a binary fraction, good for about sixteen significant digits. Line seven works on the quantity, three. Times two is six, an int. Then come three ways to divide it by two. A single slash is true division, and always gives a float, one point five. A double slash is floor division, one. The percent sign is the remainder, also one. And double star, as you saw, is a power. Now the price. Line nine multiplies nine ninety-five by three, and the terminal prints twenty-nine point eight four nine nine nine, and so on, ending in eight. Not twenty-nine eighty-five. Lines ten and eleven show the same thing in its most famous form: point one plus point two prints point three, followed by a long run of zeros and a four, and asking whether it equals point three gives False. This is not a Python bug. Most decimal fractions, including point one, have no exact binary representation, just as one third has no exact decimal one. A float holds the nearest binary fraction it can, and the tiny error shows up when you add or multiply. For a measurement, a temperature or a weight in grams, that error is far below anything that matters. For money, it is not acceptable: a report that is out by a fraction of a cent on every line will eventually be out by real cents, and nobody will trust it. The note on the right says it plainly. So the next section fixes the price.

Python's standard library has a type made for exactly this problem: Decimal, from the decimal module, imported on line three. A Decimal works in base ten, the way an accountant does, so nine ninety-five is exactly nine ninety-five. The one rule is how you create it: from a string, with quotes, as on line ten. Then price times three is exactly twenty-nine eighty-five, and the first line of output shows it. Lines five and six add two constants: the sales tax rate, eight point eight seven five percent, and one cent. The names are in capitals, which is Python's convention for a value that should never change. Python does not enforce it; it is a promise to the reader. Line twelve computes the tax. Twenty-nine eighty-five times the rate is two point six four nine one eight seven five, which is not an amount anyone can pay, so quantize rounds it to the cent. And it says how to round. Decimal's default is to round halves to the nearest even digit, which is a fine rule for statistics but not what a till receipt does, so we name ROUND HALF UP. Tax is two sixty-five, and the total is thirty-two fifty, exactly. Line fifteen asks the old question again, and this time point one plus point two does equal point three. Line sixteen shows the trap: build a Decimal from the float nine point nine five, without quotes, and you get the float's error, faithfully copied, all forty-nine digits of it. Finally line seventeen multiplies the price by the float one point five, and Python refuses, with a TypeError. That is deliberate. Mixing an exact type with an approximate one would quietly reintroduce the error we just removed, so Decimal makes you choose. From here on, every amount in the pipeline is a Decimal, from the moment it is read.

Every product in the roastery has a stock code, a SKU, and in this shop it encodes two facts: the origin, E T H for Ethiopia, and the size of the bag in grams. The pipeline will need both, and both live inside a string. The editor has folded away the constants from the last section; the new lines are highlighted. A string is a sequence of characters, and each one has a position. The table on the right lays out E T H dash two fifty: indexes zero to six from the start, and minus one to minus seven from the end. So sku zero is E, sku minus one is the last character, zero, and len counts seven characters. That is the first line of output. Line fifteen takes a slice. sku up to three means from the start up to, but not including, index three, which is E T H. Python's slices always stop before their end, which is why the length of a slice is simply end minus start. Line sixteen slices from index four to the end, two fifty, but that is still text. To use it as a number, int converts it, and grams times quantity is seven hundred and fifty grams. Line nineteen shows two string methods: split breaks the SKU at the dash into a list of two parts, and upper gives the name in capitals. Note the word gives. A string can never be changed; upper returns a new string and leaves name as it was. Line twenty is an f-string: put an f before the quotes and anything in braces is replaced by its value, here the quantity, the name, the grams and the Decimal total, in dollars. And the last line is a warning for later. Two fifty in quotes, times two, is not five hundred: it is the text repeated, two fifty two fifty. Every value in a CSV file arrives as text like this, which is why reading files, in course six, always converts first.

Some facts about an order are yes or no, and some are simply missing. Python has a type for each. Line fifteen asks whether this order is wholesale, meaning ten bags or more. The comparison quantity greater than or equal to ten produces a bool, one of exactly two values, True or False, and the first line of output shows False and its type. Comparisons like this produce bools, and in the next course they will drive every decision the pipeline makes. Line fourteen is different. Most orders have no coupon, and we need to say so. Not with zero, which is a number, or an empty string, which is text, but with None: Python's value for no value at all. There is exactly one None object in a running program, so the right way to test for it is with is, the identity check you met in the last course. coupon is None prints True, and its type is NoneType. Next, a rule that Python uses everywhere: every value can be asked whether it counts as true. Line nineteen tries four. Zero is false, three is true, the empty string is false, and a non-empty one is true. The table on the right adds the rest of the pattern: None and an empty list are false too. Empty or zero means false; anything else means true. That lets the next course write if orders, rather than if the length of orders is greater than zero. The last line is the reason None needs care. Call upper on the coupon, as if it were a string, and the program stops with an AttributeError: NoneType object has no attribute upper. This is one of the most common errors in real Python code. A value that may be missing will, one day, be missing, and the code that uses it must check first. We will, with an if, in the very next course.

One order is not a day. The pipeline needs to hold many values in sequence, and Python's general-purpose container for that is the list. Line three writes one in square brackets: four SKUs, in the order they were sold. Line four writes the quantities, in the same order. A list can change. Lines six and seven append a fifth sale to each, and the table on the right shows both lists afterwards, with each position's index counted from the start and from the end, exactly as with a string. The output reads the lists in several ways. len gives five items, sku zero is the first, sku minus one the last. A slice of a list is a new list, and one to three gives the items at index one and two. The in operator asks whether a value is present, and count says how many times: E T H two fifty was sold twice. On the same line, sum adds up the quantities: eleven bags in all. The last line asks for index five. The list has five items, numbered zero to four, so there is no index five, and Python stops with an IndexError: list index out of range. It never quietly hands back nothing. That is a choice Python makes again and again, and it is the right one for a pipeline: a wrong answer that looks right is far worse than a clear error. Now look again at the two lists, and at the note on the right. The third SKU only makes sense with the third quantity. They are one record, split across two lists that must stay in step, and the first time someone appends to one and forgets the other, every row after that is wrong. The fix is to keep each record together, which is what the next section does.

A tuple is Python's way of keeping a few values together as one fixed record. It is written with round brackets, and here each one is a whole order: an order ID, a SKU and a quantity. The list orders holds three of them, one per row, which is exactly the shape the table on the right shows. The record can no longer drift apart: the quantity travels with its SKU. You can index into a tuple like a list. orders one is the second row, and orders one, one is its SKU, C O L five hundred. But the real way to use a tuple is to unpack it. Line nine has three names on the left and one tuple on the right, and Python assigns them position by position: order ID, sku and quantity, which the first line of output shows. When a function in the next course hands back several values at once, this is how you will receive them. Line twelve adds the starred form. first, star rest equals orders puts the first row into first, and collects everything left over into a list called rest. The output shows the first order's ID, then that rest holds two rows, the last being order one thousand and three. The final line tries to change a tuple, setting the first order's quantity to four, and Python refuses: tuple object does not support item assignment. This is the difference between the two. A list is a collection that grows and changes; a tuple is one record whose shape is fixed. That makes tuples safe to pass around, and, as you will see with sets, safe to use as keys. But a tuple has a weakness for our orders. Its fields have positions, not names, and orders zero, two says nothing about what two means. The next section gives every field a name.

The dictionary is the most important container in Python, and in the pipeline it does two jobs. The first is the catalogue, on line five. A dict is written in curly braces as pairs of a key and a value, and here each key is a SKU and each value its price, as a Decimal, of course. The second job is the order itself, on line ten. It is also a dict, but now the keys are field names: id, sku and quantity. Compared with the tuple, nothing is a position any more; every field says what it is. Line twelve uses both together. order square bracket sku reads the order's SKU, and the catalogue looks that SKU up to find its price: nine ninety-five, and for three bags, twenty-nine eighty-five. A lookup like this does not scan the catalogue from the top. A dict hashes the key, which takes it straight to the right slot, so finding one product among five or among five million takes about the same time. Line fourteen asks how many entries the catalogue holds, three, and whether C O L five hundred is a key, True. Then it looks up a product that is not there yet. get returns None instead of failing, which is the safe way to ask about a key that may be missing. Line fifteen adds that product, simply by assigning to a new key. Listing the catalogue shows the four keys in the order they were added: dicts keep insertion order, a language guarantee since Python 3.7. Finally, square brackets with a key that does not exist, P E R two fifty, stop the program with a KeyError that names the missing key. That is what will happen when a day's file mentions a product the catalogue does not know, and in course six the pipeline will catch it and report the row, instead of crashing.

The roastery wants to know how many different customers ordered today, and who was new. A list of orders cannot answer that directly, because a customer who orders three times appears three times. The container for distinct values is the set. Line six turns today's six orders into a set, and the duplicates simply disappear. The first line of output shows six orders and three customers. Line three writes yesterday's set directly, in curly braces, like a dict without values. A set is built on the same hashing as a dict's keys, which gives it two strengths. The first is membership: asking whether omar is in today's set, or raj, is one hash lookup, however large the set grows, where the same question of a list checks every item in turn. In course eleven, that difference turns a slow pipeline into a fast one. The second strength is set algebra, and the table on the right lays it out. today ampersand yesterday is the intersection: customers who came back, lena and maya. today minus yesterday is the difference: the new customer, raj. And the bar is the union: everyone who ordered on either day. Notice the word sorted around each one. A set has no order. The order Python prints a set of strings in can even change from one run to the next, so whenever the output matters, as in a report, sort it first. The last line answers a question every beginner asks. If curly braces make a set, what is an empty pair of them? The answer is a dict; dicts had the braces first. An empty set is written set with brackets. One rule applies to everything you put in a set or use as a dict key: it must not change, which is why a tuple can be a key and a list cannot. That rule matters in the final section of this course.

Real orders have more than one product, so the final shape nests one container in another. On line five, an order is a dict, and its lines key holds a list of line items, each itself a dict with a SKU and a quantity. This is the shape the pipeline will build from every day's file, and it is also the shape of most JSON you will ever read. Nesting is where the first idea of this course pays off: names, and the values inside containers, are references to objects. Lines eleven to thirteen make three things that look like copies. same equals order copies nothing at all: it is a second name for the same dict. order dot copy makes a new dict, but a shallow one: its values are the same objects as the original's, including the same list of lines. And copy dot deepcopy, from the copy module, copies everything, all the way down. Now line fourteen changes the customer through same, and line fifteen appends a line item through shallow. The output tells the story. The original order's customer is now omar, because same is order. And the original now has two line items, although we only touched shallow, because shallow's lines and order's lines are one list. Only deep still has one. The last line confirms it: same is order, True; shallow is order, False; but shallow's lines is order's lines, True. The picture on the right is the state after line fifteen: four names, three dicts and two lists, and the list shown in red is reachable from two of the dicts. Most bugs of the form I changed one thing and another changed too are exactly this, and the table underneath is the rule for avoiding them. That completes the data the pipeline needs to hold. Next course, it starts processing it.

The last course gave the pipeline its data: a catalogue of prices, and orders as dictionaries. This course makes it do something with that data, and the first step is the smallest unit of work in Python: the expression. An expression is anything that computes a value. Line fifteen looks up the price for this order's SKU, line sixteen multiplies it by the quantity, and line seventeen works out the sales tax on that, rounded to the cent. The first line of output shows the line total, fifty-two fifty, the tax, four sixty-six, and the two added together. Each of those lines is one expression, built from smaller ones joined by operators. When an expression has several operators, Python needs to know which to apply first, and the table on the right lists the order, tightest first. Line nineteen shows why it matters. Two plus three times four is fourteen, because multiplication binds tighter than addition, and brackets change it to twenty. Minus two, to the power of two, is minus four, not four, because the power is applied before the minus sign. When in doubt, add brackets: they cost nothing and the next reader will thank you. Line twenty shows two kinds of expression that produce True or False. One is less than or equal to the quantity, less than or equal to fifty, is a chained comparison, and reads exactly as it would in maths. And the or operator combines two tests: True if either side is true. Python also stops early: if the left side of an or is already true, the right side is never evaluated. Finally, line twenty-two uses an augmented assignment. day total plus equals line total is short for day total equals day total plus line total. With Decimals, it builds a new object and rebinds the name, exactly as you saw in the last course. Next, using those True and False values to make decisions.

The roastery has discount rules, and the table on the right sets them out. Ten bags or more is a wholesale order, with fifteen percent off. Otherwise, an order worth fifty dollars or more gets five percent. Anything else pays full price. Rules like these are what an if statement is for. Line sixteen tests the first rule. If quantity is at least ten, the indented line under it runs, and the discount is fifteen percent. The indentation is not decoration: in Python, the indented block is what belongs to the if, and it ends where the indentation does. Line eighteen is an elif, short for else if. Its test is only tried when everything above it was false. And else, on line twenty, catches every case that no test claimed. Python works down the chain and takes the first branch whose test is true, then skips the rest, so exactly one discount is ever chosen. That ordering matters. A wholesale order of twelve bags is also worth more than fifty dollars, and because the wholesale test comes first, it gets the bigger discount, which is what the shop wants. This order is three bags of Colombian at seventeen fifty. That is not wholesale, so the first test is false. The subtotal is fifty-two fifty, so the elif is true, and the discount is five percent. The first line of output shows it: subtotal, discount, and the line total of forty-nine eighty-eight, the forty-nine eight seven five rounded half up to the cent. The last two lines show a shorter kind of test. if not order dot get coupon: the order has no coupon key, so get returns None, and None counts as false, so not makes it true. A missing coupon and an empty one are treated the same, which is exactly what we want. Right now these rules run for one order. Before we loop them over a day, one more way to decide.

Not every row the shop sends is a sale. Some are refunds, and one day there will be a row type nobody planned for. The pipeline needs to look at a row, work out what kind of thing it is, and pull out the fields that kind has. An if chain can do that, but Python has a statement built for exactly this job: match, added in Python 3.10. The row on line five is a refund, against an earlier order, for nine ninety-five. Line seven matches it against a list of cases, tried from the top, and the first one that fits wins. Each case is a pattern, and a pattern describes a shape. The first case, on line eight, is a dictionary whose type is sale, with a SKU that is a string and a quantity that is an int. That is three checks at once: the keys must be there, the type must be sale, and the values must have the right types. Then if qty greater than zero is a guard, an extra condition the pattern must also pass. Our row's type is refund, so this case does not match. The second case does. Its type is refund, and it has order and amount keys. And here is the part an if chain cannot do neatly: the names order ID and amount in the pattern are bound to the values found in the row, so the line underneath can use them straight away. The terminal shows: refund, nine ninety-five, against order zero nine nine eight. A mapping pattern only asks for the keys it names, so extra keys in the row are fine. The third case catches any row with a type we do not know, and binds that type to kind so we can report it. And the last case, a single underscore, matches anything at all, including something that is not a row. The table on the right lists the four cases in order. Next, running rules like these over every order of the day.

So far the discount rules have priced one order. A day has many, and the for loop is how Python does the same work for each item in a collection. Line twenty reads almost like English: for order in orders. The list is folded away above, but the table on the right shows its four orders. Python takes the first dictionary, binds the name order to it, and runs the indented block. Then it binds order to the second dictionary and runs the block again, and so on, until the list is exhausted. The block is everything indented under the for line, and inside it you can see the rules from section two, unchanged: the same if, elif and else, now running once per order. Each pass computes the amount, adds it to the day total on line thirty, and prints one line. The terminal shows the result of all four passes, and the table on the right explains each one. Order one thousand and one is three bags of Ethiopian, under fifty dollars, so no discount. One thousand and two is twelve bags, wholesale, fifteen percent off. One thousand and three is two bags of Kenyan at thirty-one dollars, which is sixty-two, so five percent off. And one thousand and four is a single bag. Every branch of the rules has now run, on real orders. Notice where day total lives. It is set to zero on line nineteen, before the loop, so it survives every pass and accumulates. If that line were inside the loop, it would be reset to zero four times, and the total would only ever show the last order. Line thirty-two is not indented, so it runs once, after the loop has finished: a day total of two hundred and seventy-seven dollars twenty. That is the first real number our pipeline has produced. Next, loops that stop early, and loops that skip.

A for loop runs once for each item in a collection that already exists. Sometimes the job is different: keep going until something changes. That is a while loop. On line six, while queue means: as long as the queue is not empty, run the block again. An empty list counts as false, as you saw in the last course, so the loop ends by itself when the queue runs out. Line seven takes the first row off the front of the queue with pop zero, so every pass shrinks the list. Each row here is raw text, the way an old till exports orders, and line eleven splits it at the commas and unpacks it into three names, using the tuple unpacking from the last course. Two keywords steer the loop from inside. The first is continue. On line twelve, a row with a quantity of zero is not an error, but there is nothing to price, so we print that it was skipped and continue, which jumps straight back to the top for the next row, skipping everything below it in the block. The second is break. Some exports end with a trailer row, the word END, and anything after it is not part of the day. So on line eight, when the row is END, we report how many rows remain and break, which leaves the loop at once. The terminal shows the whole story. Order one thousand and one is processed. One thousand and two is skipped. One thousand and three is processed. Then the trailer is reached, with one row after it ignored, and the final count is two. A word of caution: a while loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever. Here, pop guarantees progress, because every pass removes a row. Whenever you write a while loop, look for the line that moves it toward the end. Most of the time, a for loop is the right choice. Next, building whole lists in a single line.

A lot of loops have the same shape: start with an empty list, loop over something, and append one value per item. Python has a compact form for exactly that pattern, called a comprehension. Line seventeen builds the subtotal of every order: the expression first, then for o in orders. Read it as: the price times the quantity, for each order. The first line of output is the resulting list of four Decimals. Line nineteen adds a filter at the end. Only orders with three or more bags are included, and the expression keeps just the ID, so the output is a list of two order IDs. The same idea works for the other containers. Curly braces with a single expression, on line twenty-one, build a set, so the SKUs come out with no duplicates: three, not four, which we sort before printing because sets have no order. And curly braces with a key, a colon and a value, on line twenty-three, build a dictionary. Here it is a ten percent sale price for every product in the catalogue. The output shows Ethiopian at eight point nine five five, a reminder that a Decimal is exact but not automatically rounded to cents; the pipeline would quantize it before charging anyone. Line twenty-five is the most useful of all. With no brackets around it, inside a call to sum, the comprehension becomes a generator expression: it produces each quantity one at a time, and sum adds them up, without ever building a list. The total is eighteen bags. In course six this is exactly how we will handle files too large to hold in memory. Comprehensions are a good tool when the whole thing reads as one idea. When it needs two nested loops, an if and else in the middle, or a side effect like printing, write the ordinary for loop instead. Clear beats clever, and the reader decides which is which.

The pricing rules now appear inside a loop, and soon they will be needed in more places: when the pipeline re-prices a refund, when a test checks them, when the report shows a single order. Copying the same lines into each place would mean every future change to a discount has to be made several times, and one day someone will miss one. The answer is a function: a block of code with a name. Line twenty defines price line with the keyword def. The names in brackets, order and catalogue, are its parameters. Whatever the caller passes in is bound to those names for the duration of the call. Line twenty-one is a docstring, a string that describes what the function does, and Python keeps it with the function: the last line of output prints it back. The body, from line twenty-two, is the same rules as before, folded by the editor. And line thirty uses return to hand the result back to whoever called the function. When return runs, the function ends. Now look at the loop on line thirty-five. It no longer knows anything about discounts. It calls price line with an order and the catalogue, and gets a line total back. The output is the same as in section four, order by order, with the same day total of two hundred and seventy-seven twenty, which is the point: we changed the structure, not the behaviour. There is one more benefit, and it matters a great deal later. The names quantity, subtotal and discount are local to the function. They exist only while it runs, so they cannot collide with any other part of the program. A function is a small, sealed unit with inputs and an output, and that is exactly what can be tested, which is what course ten will do. Next, the different ways of passing arguments, and a trap that catches almost everyone once.

When you call a function, there are several ways to match the values you pass to its parameters. The function on line eight, line total, takes a price, a quantity, and a discount. The first call, on line eighteen, passes all three by position: the first value goes to price, the second to quantity, the third to discount. Twelve bags at seventeen fifty, with fifteen percent off, is one hundred and seventy-eight fifty, the same as the loop gave us. The second call, on line nineteen, uses keyword arguments: quantity equals two, price equals thirty-one dollars. With names, the order no longer matters, and the call explains itself. And it leaves out the discount entirely, because the definition gives it a default value of zero. The output is sixty-two dollars, full price. Defaults make the common case short and the unusual case possible. Now the trap. The function add line, on line thirteen, has a default too: an empty list. The idea is that each call without a list starts a new one. The first call, on line twenty, adds Ethiopian and returns a list with one item, as expected. But the second call, which should start fresh, returns two items: Ethiopian and Colombian. The cause is when the default is made. Python evaluates a default once, when the def statement runs, and stores it on the function object. The last line of output proves it: the function's defaults attribute holds that very list, now containing both items. The picture on the right shows the state: the function's defaults and both calls refer to one list, shown in red. Any default that can be changed, a list, a dict or a set, is shared across every call. The fix, in the note underneath, is the standard idiom: default to None, and inside the function, if lines is None, create a new empty list. Immutable defaults, like numbers, strings and Decimals, are always safe. Next, where Python looks for a name.

Inside price line, the names quantity and discount existed only during the call. That raises a general question: when Python meets a name, where does it look for it? The answer has four places, searched in a fixed order known as L E G B: local, enclosing, global and builtin. The table on the right maps them onto this file. Line three creates TAX at the top of the module, which makes it a global. The function outer, on line six, assigns its own TAX, which is local to outer. And inside outer is another function, inner, which assigns a local called where, and returns where together with TAX. inner has no TAX of its own, so Python looks in the enclosing function, finds outer's TAX, and stops. The first match wins. The output's first line shows both: the global TAX, printed at the top level, and the tuple local, enclosing, from inner. The fourth scope is builtin: names like len, print and sum, which are always there. Line seventeen calls len on an order ID and gets eight. Then line eighteen does something every Python programmer does by accident at least once. It assigns the number eight to the name len. That creates a global called len, and globals are searched before builtins, so the builtin len is now hidden. Line nineteen tries to call it, and Python stops with a TypeError: int object is not callable. The fix is simply never to use a builtin's name for your own variable: sum, list, id, type and input are the usual victims. The note at the bottom shows the opposite surprise, and it is the real message from Python 3.14. If a function assigns to a name anywhere in its body, that name is local for the whole function. So processed plus equals one, on a global processed, fails with an UnboundLocalError. The clean answer is not the global keyword, but to return the value instead. Next, errors you expect.

Real input is messy. The table on the right shows four rows as they will arrive from a file, with every value as text. Two of them are fine. One names a product, P E R two fifty, that is not in the catalogue, and one has the quantity spelt out as the word two. In the last course, either of these stopped the whole program, with a KeyError and a ValueError. For a pipeline, that is the wrong behaviour: one bad row out of thousands should be reported, not allowed to stop the day. The tool for this is the try statement. On line nineteen, try marks the line that might fail: the catalogue lookup and the conversion of the quantity to an int. If either raises an exception, Python abandons the rest of the try block and looks at the except clauses in order. Line twenty-one handles a KeyError, an unknown SKU, by recording the row and the reason in the bad list. Line twenty-three handles a ValueError, a quantity that is not a number, the same way. as error binds the exception object, so its message can be kept. Then, on line twenty-five, else runs only if the try block raised nothing at all, and that is where the good row is recorded. Keeping the success path in else, rather than inside try, means the try covers only the line we expect to fail. The output shows the result: two rows priced, at twenty-nine eighty-five and sixty-two dollars, and two rejected, each with its order ID and the reason. The run carried on past both. Notice what is not here: a bare except, with no exception named. That would catch everything, including a typo in our own code, and hide it as if it were a bad row. Always name the exceptions you expect. Anything else is a bug, and it should stop the program loudly. Next, raising exceptions of our own.

Python raises KeyError and ValueError when something is wrong with how a value is used. But some rows are wrong in ways Python cannot know about. A quantity of minus two is a perfectly good integer. Without a check, it would be priced: minus two bags of Colombian is minus thirty-five dollars, a silent refund that nobody asked for, quietly lowering the day's revenue. The note on the right puts it plainly. A clear error is always better than a wrong answer. So the pipeline defines its own error. Line three creates InvalidOrder. The class keyword is covered properly in course nine; for now, read this line as: a new kind of ValueError, with our own name. Because it is a kind of ValueError, code that catches ValueError will catch it too. The function validate, on line seven, checks one business rule: the quantity must be positive. If it is not, line nine raises an InvalidOrder, with a message that names the order. raise stops the function immediately and hands the exception up to whoever called it. The loop on line fourteen validates both rows, and on line seventeen it catches InvalidOrder by name. Order one thousand and one is valid, so validate simply returns and nothing is printed. Order one thousand and eight is rejected, and the terminal shows the message we wrote. Then the last line calls validate on a row with a quantity of zero, outside any try. Nothing catches it, so the exception travels all the way up and stops the program, and the traceback shows the call, then the raise inside validate, and finally the error's own name: InvalidOrder, order one thousand and seven, quantity must be positive. Anyone reading that knows exactly what was wrong, and where. That completes the core of processing. The pipeline can compute, decide, loop, name its steps and handle bad rows. Next course, it reads its rows from real files.

Until now, the pipeline's orders were typed into the code. Real orders arrive as files. The explorer shows the project's new data folder: inside data slash raw is the catalogue, and the shop's first file, the orders for the first of October, one line per order. This course is about getting that data into Python, safely and correctly. The tool is open. Line five opens the file and hands back a file object, which is a stream of text you read from the start. Two things about that line matter. First, the encoding. A file on disk is bytes, and the encoding says how those bytes become characters. Always name it. In Python 3.14 the default still depends on the computer the code runs on, so code that works on your laptop can fail on a server; the note on the right says so. The second thing is the word with. Line six reads the first line, the header, and line seven prints its repr, so you can see the newline character at the end of it, which every line read from a file still carries. Then line eight loops over the file itself. A file object hands out one line per pass, so even a file far larger than your memory can be read this way, a line at a time. Line nine strips the newline and prints each order, and there they are in the terminal: six orders, including one whose quantity is spelled out as three, and one customer, Luna Café Limited, whose name contains a comma. Both will matter shortly. Now the last line. The with block has ended, and f dot closed is True. That is the promise with makes: however the block ends, normally, through a return, or through an exception, the file is closed. Open files are a limited resource, and a file left open for writing may never be fully saved. With makes closing automatic, so it is how every file in this course is opened. Next, what those bytes really are.

The second day's file came from the shop's old till, and it is the first file that will not open the way the first one did. To see why, this time we open it in binary mode, with the letters r b on line five. In binary mode Python does not decode anything; it hands back bytes, exactly what is on the disk. The first line of output says the object is bytes, a hundred and forty-five of them, and the second shows the file's last line as bytes. Look at the customer's name: z, o, then a backslash x e b. That is a single byte, e b, standing for e with two dots. On line ten we ask Python to decode the bytes as UTF-8, the standard encoding of the web, of Python source files, and of almost everything written today. It fails. In UTF-8, a byte like e nine must be followed by two more of a special kind, and the first one Python meets, at position sixty, the e with an accent in josé, is followed by a comma. The old till wrote its files in Windows code page twelve fifty-two, a single-byte encoding from the nineteen nineties. The table on the right shows the difference: in twelve fifty-two each of these letters is one byte, in UTF-8 it is two. Line fourteen decodes with the right encoding, and now we have a str: text, a hundred and forty-five characters, and the name prints correctly. Bytes are what is stored; a str is text, and decode is the bridge between them, always through a named encoding. A wrong guess is not always an error, either: decoding UTF-8 bytes as twelve fifty-two usually succeeds, and just garbles the accents. So the rule is to convert once, at the boundary. Lines seventeen and eighteen write the text straight back, encoded as UTF-8, and the last line of output shows the same name, now stored as two bytes, c three a b. From here on, every file in the pipeline is UTF-8. Next, finding all the files.

A third day's file has arrived, and soon there will be one a day. The pipeline should not need a line of code per file; it should find them. The standard library's pathlib module treats a path as an object rather than a string, and that makes finding and handling files much cleaner. Line five creates RAW, a Path pointing at the data slash raw folder. The first line of output asks whether it exists and whether it is a directory: True and True. Line eight is the important one. glob takes a pattern, orders dash star dot csv, where star matches anything, and returns every matching path in the folder. The catalogue does not match, so it is left out. sorted puts the days in order. That works because the file names use ISO dates, year then month then day, which sort correctly as plain text. If the shop had named them day, month, year, the sort would be wrong, which is one reason to insist on ISO dates whenever you can. The loop prints each file's name and its size in bytes, read from the file system with stat. Then line twelve takes the first path apart. The stem is the name without its extension, the suffix is dot csv, and the parent is the folder it lives in. The table on the right sets these out. Line thirteen pulls the date out of the stem by removing the prefix orders dash, which leaves two thousand and twenty-six, ten, oh one. Line fourteen shows the slash operator: RAW slash catalogue dot json builds a new path, with the right separator for the operating system, so the same code runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. And the last line prints the current working directory. Relative paths like data slash raw are measured from there, which is why the pipeline is always run from the project folder. Next, reading these files properly, as CSV.

Each order file is CSV: comma-separated values, with a header row naming the columns. It is tempting to read one by splitting each line at its commas. Look at the last order of the day to see why that fails. The customer is Luna Café, Limited, and that comma is part of the name. In the file, the name is wrapped in double quotes so that the comma inside it is data, not a separator. A plain split cuts the name in two and shifts every column after it, as the note on the right warns. The standard library's csv module understands quoting, escaping and line endings, so it is the right tool. Line seven opens the file with one extra argument: newline equals the empty string. It tells Python to leave line endings alone and let the csv module handle them, which is what the csv documentation asks for. Line eight wraps the file in a DictReader. A DictReader reads the header row itself, and line nine prints what it found: the five field names. Then every following row comes back as a dictionary, keyed by those names. Line ten collects them into a list. The loop prints three fields from each row, and the output shows two things. Luna Café, Limited, arrived as one field, comma and all. And every quantity is shown in quotes. That is the lesson of the last line of output: every value read from a CSV file is a string. Three is the text three, and the word three is just as much a string as the digit, so a CSV file can never promise you a number. Converting each value to the right type, and deciding what to do when it will not convert, is the pipeline's job. Reading row by name, row square bracket sku, instead of by position, also means the code keeps working if the shop ever adds or reorders columns. Next, the catalogue, which is not CSV at all.

The catalogue, the list of products and their prices, comes from the shop's website, and it is JSON: JavaScript Object Notation, the format most web services speak. JSON has a handful of types, and the table on the right shows what each becomes in Python. An object, in curly braces, becomes a dict. An array becomes a list. Strings become str, and true, false and null become True, False and None. Line nine reads the whole file with json dot load. The first line of output shows the result: a dict with four entries, keyed by SKU, in the order they appear in the file. The second line shows one entry, itself a dict, with the product's name and its price. Now look closely at that price. It is in quotes. Whoever wrote this catalogue stored every price as a string, and that was the right decision. Line thirteen turns it into a Decimal, and nine ninety-five times three is exactly twenty-nine eighty-five. The next line shows what happens otherwise. If the price had been stored as a plain JSON number, json dot loads would turn it into a float, and multiplying by three would give the same long, slightly wrong number you met in course four. The format itself is not the problem; the type it is read into is. And when you do not control the file, there is a fix on the last line: the parse float argument tells the json module to build every number with a decimal point as a Decimal instead of a float, and the answer is exact again. Between the CSV files and this catalogue, everything the pipeline needs to read is now in Python. But reading is not trusting. Some of those rows are wrong, and the next section decides what happens to them.

Reading the day's file gave us six rows.
