Two of them should never be priced: order one thousand and four, whose quantity is the word three, and order one thousand and five, for a product the catalogue does not contain. The pipeline has three choices. It could crash on the first bad row, which loses the whole day for one typo. It could skip bad rows quietly, which is worse, because the report would be wrong and nobody would know. Or it can keep the good rows, set the bad ones aside, and say exactly what it set aside and why. That is the rule for every pipeline in this course: never stop silently, and never drop silently. The function validate, on line fourteen, checks one row against the business rules. If the SKU is not in the catalogue, it raises the InvalidRow error from line sixteen, which, like InvalidOrder in the last course, is a kind of ValueError with our own name. If the quantity is not made only of digits, or is zero, line eighteen raises it too, with the bad value in the message. And if both checks pass, it returns a clean copy of the row, with the quantity converted to a real int, which no later stage will ever need to convert again. The loop on line twenty-six reads the CSV and counts lines as it goes. enumerate, starting at two, gives each row its line number in the file, because the header is line one, so that a rejection can point a person straight at the line to fix. Each row is validated inside a try; good rows go into one list, and rejected ones, with their line number, ID and reason, into another. The output says four good rows and two rejected, then lists each rejection. The table on the right shows the whole day, line by line. Next, reading not one day, but the whole month, without running out of memory.

The shop has now sent the whole of October: thirty-one files, nearly six thousand orders. That still fits in memory, but a year, or a bigger shop, will not, and the pipeline should not care how many rows there are. The tool for that is a generator. Look at read rows, on line ten. It looks like an ordinary function, but on line thirteen it uses yield from instead of return, and that one word changes everything. A function that yields is a generator function. Calling it, on line twenty-one, runs none of its code. It just creates a generator object, which the first line of output shows. The code inside runs only when something asks for the next value. next, on the next line, does exactly that: the function starts, opens the first file, reads the header, yields the first row, order one thousand and one, and then pauses, right there, with the file still open and its place remembered. Ask again and it resumes from that point. The diagram on the right shows the shape of it. sum pulls a value, read rows resumes, yields one row, and pauses again. At any moment there is one open file and one row in flight, however long the month is. Line twenty-six adds a generator expression that filters out the rows whose quantity is not a number, and line twenty-seven sums the rest: the month's total bags. Nothing in that chain ever builds a list. Python's tracemalloc module measured the peak memory, and the table on the right shows the difference, read from the same run: the streamed version peaked at well under a megabyte, while line thirty, which builds a list of every row, needed more than two megabytes, and that number grows with every day added, while the streamed one does not. That is the whole of extract: real files, read safely, decoded correctly, parsed properly, validated honestly, and streamed. Next course, we aggregate them.

The pipeline can now read a whole month of orders, clean and validated. The next question the roastery asks is simple: how much did each coffee earn in October? Answering it means grouping, collecting rows that share a value, here the SKU, and combining them, here by adding up their totals. First, notice what is folded at the top of the editor. Everything from the last course, reading the files, validating each row, and setting the bad ones aside, is still there, collapsed into one function, month rows. It also prices each row with the discount rules from course five, so every row arrives with its total already worked out. The bad rows, seventy-nine of them in October, go into the rejected list, and the last line of output reports them, so nothing is lost quietly. Now the grouping itself. It uses nothing but a dictionary. revenue starts empty. For each row, we take its SKU. If that SKU is not yet a key, we create it, with a total of zero. Then we add this row's total to it. One pass over nearly six thousand rows, and the dictionary holds exactly four entries: one running total per product. The terminal prints them, in the order each product was first seen, followed by the month's revenue, just over four hundred and one thousand dollars, the sum of the four totals. This pattern, a dict of running totals keyed by the thing you are grouping by, is one of the most common in all of data processing. In SQL it is GROUP BY; in pandas it is groupby; in Spark it is the same idea spread across machines. Here it is four lines of plain Python, and it is worth writing by hand once, so the tools later never feel like magic. The only clumsy part is that if, which every key needs before its first addition. The next section removes it.

The if statement in the last section had one job: make sure a key exists before adding to it. That job is so common that the standard library's collections module has two containers that do it for you, and this file uses both. The import at the top brings in Counter and defaultdict. A defaultdict is a dictionary with a factory: a function it calls to create the value for any key that is missing. revenue is a defaultdict of Decimal. The first time a SKU appears, the dictionary calls Decimal with no arguments, which gives zero, stores it, and the addition goes ahead. The first line of output shows that Decimal on its own really is zero, and that Ethiopian's total is the same as before. The if has disappeared, and the loop is now one line per figure. customers is a defaultdict of set. Each missing key starts as an empty set, and adding a customer to a set ignores repeats, so at the end each product has its set of distinct customers. All twelve of the shop's customers bought every coffee at least once in October, which the last line shows. bags is a Counter, a dictionary specialised for counting. A missing key reads as zero, which the third line shows for P E R two fifty, the product that does not exist, but unlike a defaultdict, asking does not add the key: P E R two fifty is still not in the Counter. And Counter has a method made for reports: most common. Asked for the top two, it returns Kenyan and Ethiopian by bags sold, as pairs of product and count. Notice that this ranking differs from revenue, because Kenyan bags are much larger. The table on the right compares what each container does with a missing key. Reach for defaultdict when you are collecting, and for Counter when you are counting. Next, putting the results in order.

A report should put the most important line first. That means sorting, and the built-in sorted function, which takes any collection and returns a new list in order. The interesting part is the key argument. Sorting pairs of product and revenue would, by default, compare the pairs by their first item, the SKU, which gives alphabetical order. We want them ordered by revenue. key is a function that sorted calls on each item, to get the value to compare by. lambda item, colon, item one, is a function written inline, with no name: given a pair, it returns the second element, the revenue. With reverse equals True, the largest comes first. The terminal shows the result: Kenyan first, at nearly a hundred and seventy-one thousand dollars, then Colombian, Brazilian and Ethiopian. Ethiopian sold more bags than Colombian or Brazilian, but at nine ninety-five a bag it earned the least. The next line sorts customers instead, and uses a key that is not a lambda at all. by customer dot get is a method that takes a name and returns that customer's total, which is exactly what sorted needs, so we can pass it directly. Slicing the result with square brackets, colon three keeps the top three customers. The last two lines show a trap. Sorting three names by plain comparison puts Luna Café, Limited, first, before ana, because Python compares the characters' code points, and every capital letter comes before every lowercase one. Passing key equals str dot lower compares the lowercase versions instead, and the order becomes what a person would expect. The list on the right gathers the rules. One more is worth knowing: sorted always returns a new list, while a list's own sort method reorders that list in place and returns None, which is a classic source of bugs when someone writes x equals x dot sort. Next, the averages and the rounding.

A summary is more than totals. The shop also wants to know what a typical order is worth, and the standard library's statistics module answers that. This file collects every line total of the month into a list, five thousand seven hundred and ninety-seven Decimals. statistics dot mean adds them up and divides by the count. It works with Decimals and keeps them exact, so the first line of output shows the mean to twenty-eight significant digits, Decimal's default precision. The median is the middle value when the totals are sorted, forty-eight seventy-five, and the mode is the most common value, seventeen fifty, which is one bag of Colombian. Notice that the mean, about sixty-nine dollars, is well above the median. A few large wholesale orders pull the mean up, while the median shrugs them off. Which one tells the truth about a typical order depends on the question, so a good report often shows both. Now rounding. The mean has to be shown in cents, so the code rounds it once, at the end, with quantize and half up: sixty-nine twenty-five. That is the rule: round once, for display or payment, and never in the middle of a calculation, where small errors add up. The next two lines are the reason to be careful about how you round. The built-in round, given the float two point six seven five, returns two point six seven. That float is actually stored as slightly less than two point six seven five, so it rounds down. The Decimal, rounded half up, gives two point six eight. And round itself rounds halves to the nearest even digit, not up: round of nought point five is zero, and round of one point five is two. The table on the right sets out all three. Finally, math dot ceil always rounds up, which is what packing needs: the month's bags fill one thousand nine hundred and forty-two boxes of twelve, the last one not quite full. Next, dates.

Every row carries its date, but as text, two thousand and twenty-six, dash, ten, dash, twenty-two. Text can be compared and sorted, but it cannot tell you what weekday that was, which week it falls in, or what the date is a week later. For that, the date has to become a date object, and the datetime module provides it. date dot fromisoformat parses the ISO text into a date. The first loop totals revenue per day, keyed by real dates. max with key equals by day dot get finds the best day of the month, the same trick as in the sorting section, and strftime formats it: percent A means the full weekday name. The best day was Thursday the twenty-second of October, with over seventeen thousand dollars. Weekly totals need a definition of week, and the safest is the international standard, ISO 8601: weeks run Monday to Sunday, and are numbered through the year. isocalendar returns a date's ISO year, week and weekday, and the second loop adds each day's total into its week. The terminal shows five weeks, from forty to forty-four. Week forty looks small, but the table on the right explains why: that week began on Monday the twenty-eighth of September, so only four of its days are in October. Week forty-four, similarly, ends on the first of November. A report that compares weeks must say so, or it will make the first week of every month look like a slump. The last line shows date arithmetic. Adding a timedelta of seven days to the best day gives the twenty-ninth, the same weekday one week later. And subtracting one date from another gives a timedelta too, whose days attribute is the gap: nine days from the best day to the end of the month. These are calendar dates, with no time and no time zone, which is all daily files need. When timestamps arrive, the same module has datetime and zoneinfo. Next, tools for grouping without building lists.

Every aggregation so far used a dictionary that grew as rows went past. The itertools module offers another approach for data that arrives in order, and it never builds a list. October's rows come out of month rows in date order, because the files are read in date order. groupby takes an iterator and a key function, and yields one group per run of equal keys: here, one group per day, each group itself an iterator over that day's rows. There is a catch, and it is the most important thing about groupby: it groups neighbours only. If the same key appears again later, after a different one, it starts a new group. So the input must already be sorted by the key, as ours is. islice is slicing for iterators. Square brackets do not work on a generator, because it has no length and no positions, but islice of groupby, three, takes just the first three groups, lazily. The output shows the first three days, with four, three and three valid orders. The rest of the month is never read. chain joins iterators end to end. A late order, typed in by hand as a list of one row, is chained after the whole month, and counting the combined stream gives five thousand seven hundred and ninety-eight rows: the month, plus one. Nothing was copied to do it. Finally, islice with a start of three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine and no end, passed to next, skips straight to the four thousandth row, which turns out to be an order from the twenty-third. Notice that each of these lines calls month rows again. A generator can be read only once: when it has been used up, it yields nothing, so a second pass needs a fresh generator. That is the trade for using almost no memory, and it is usually a good one. The table and list on the right summarise the three tools. Next, putting it all together into the transform step.

An ETL pipeline has three stages: extract, transform, load. Extract is month rows, which reads and validates. This section writes the transform as a single function, and that function is the heart of the whole pipeline. summarise takes one day's rows, and returns one summary: how many orders, how many bags, the revenue, and the best-selling product. It makes a single pass. orders and bags are plain counters, and revenue is a Counter keyed by SKU, so the day's top product falls out at the end, picked by max with key equals revenue dot get. Then it returns a dictionary. The diagram on the right shows how it is used. month rows streams the rows, groupby from the last section splits them into days, and a dictionary comprehension calls summarise once per day, building daily: thirty-one summaries, keyed by date. The first three are printed. On the first of October there were four valid orders, twenty-one bags, and three hundred and twenty-nine dollars of revenue, mostly Colombian, thanks to the wholesale order of twelve bags. Then the month: thirty-one days, and the same four hundred and one thousand, four hundred and thirty dollars and fourteen cents as the grouping section found by a completely different route, which is a good sign that both are right. And the seventy-nine rejected rows are still counted and reported. Now notice what summarise does not do. It does not open a file, read a CSV, or print anything. It takes rows and returns a dict. That separation is deliberate, and it pays off three times. It can be reused: the same function will summarise a week or a single shop. It is easy to test: in course ten we will hand it three rows written by hand and check the answer. And it keeps each stage of the pipeline replaceable. The data has been read and transformed. Next course, it is written out, as a report and a database.

The pipeline has read October and summarised it, but so far every result has vanished the moment the program ended. The last stage of ETL is load: writing results somewhere they last. The simplest destination is a file, and the most useful file is one a person can open in a spreadsheet, so this section writes the daily summaries as CSV. Everything from the last two courses is folded at the top. The new code starts by computing the daily summaries, exactly as the transform step did. Then it makes a folder for the results. Generated files go in data slash out, kept apart from the raw data in data slash raw, so that deleting the outputs can never touch what the shop sent. mkdir with exist ok equals True creates the folder the first time and does nothing on later runs, instead of raising an error because it already exists. Then the file is opened for writing, with w, and with the same two arguments as reading: newline equals the empty string, so the csv module controls the line endings, and the encoding. csv dot writer wraps the file, and writerow writes one list as one row, adding quotes around any value that needs them, such as a customer name with a comma. The first row written is the header. Then the loop writes one row per day: the date, orders, bags, revenue, and top product. The revenue is a Decimal, and the csv module writes it as its text, three twenty-nine point zero zero, exactly. The terminal shows the result. head prints the first four lines of the new file: the header, then the first three days, matching what the transform step printed. And wc, word count, with dash l counts its lines: thirty-two, a header plus thirty-one days. The explorer on the left shows the new file, marked new, in data slash out. This report is for people to open. Next, making the same numbers readable in the terminal.

Printing a Decimal next to a word gives you the number, but not a report. Real reports line up their columns, separate thousands, and show percentages as percentages. f-strings do all of this with a small language that goes after a colon inside the braces, called the format specification. The table on the right is a short dictionary of it. The first print writes the column titles. Less than ten means left-aligned in a field ten characters wide; greater than six means right-aligned in six. Numbers are usually right-aligned, so their digits line up, and text left-aligned. The loop prints the first four days with the same widths. The revenue uses comma, point two f: a comma between every three digits, and exactly two decimal places. The fourth of October shows why the comma matters: thirteen thousand, seven hundred and thirty-nine dollars ninety-five is far easier to read with its comma. The totals line puts the whole month underneath, four hundred and one thousand, four hundred and thirty dollars fourteen, aligned with the column above it. The next line divides the rejected rows by all the rows, and point one percent formats the fraction as a percentage with one decimal: one point three percent of October's rows were rejected. Then two tools that are handy while developing. An equals sign after an expression prints the expression itself and its value, total equals Decimal, four hundred and one thousand four hundred and thirty point one four, which is a quick way to check what a variable really holds, type and all. And the last line shows a fill character: dollar, greater than fourteen pads the number on the left with dollar signs to fourteen characters, the old cheque-writing trick, and caret eleven centres a SKU. One rule to remember: formatting changes how a value is shown, never the value itself. The Decimal behind every column is still exact. Next, a format for machines rather than people.

The CSV report is for people. The roastery's website also wants the month's figures, and programs prefer JSON, because it keeps structure: a summary can hold numbers, text, and a nested dictionary of days, all in one file. The code builds that summary as an ordinary Python dictionary: the month, the total revenue, the number of rejected rows, and the daily summaries from the transform step, keyed by date. Then it tries to turn it into JSON with json dot dumps, and the terminal shows that it fails: TypeError, object of type Decimal is not JSON serializable. That error is a feature. JSON has numbers, but no exact decimal type, and the json module refuses to guess what you want. There are two ways to answer it. One is to convert every Decimal to a float, which would undo everything course four was about. The float prints as four hundred and one thousand four hundred and thirty point one four, but what it stores is a binary approximation of that, and every sum the website did with such numbers would drift. The other, used here, is the default argument. default is a function the json module calls for any value it does not know how to write, and passing str writes each Decimal as its exact text, in quotes. Any program reading the file turns those strings back into exact decimals, just as our pipeline does with the catalogue's prices. indent equals two lays the file out on several lines, indented, so a person can read it too; without it, the whole summary would be one long line. The second command in the terminal shows the top of the file: the month, the revenue in quotes, the rejected count as a plain number, and then the days, each one a nested object. Notice that the dates became keys without any help, because they are already text. Writing JSON and reading it back should always be a round trip that changes nothing, and with Decimals as strings, it is. Next, a real database.

Files are good for reports, but a business asks questions that no single report anticipated, and that is what a database is for. Python ships with SQLite, a complete SQL database that lives in one file, needs no server, and is used in more software than any other database. The table is defined in its own file, schema dot sql, shown on the right. Each order line has an ID, which is the primary key, so no two rows may share one, then the date, customer, SKU, quantity, and the total. SQLite has no exact decimal type, and its REAL type is a float, so the total is stored as TEXT, exactly as JSON stored it. The code builds the rows as lists of values, connects to data slash out slash warehouse dot db, which creates the file the first time, and runs the schema. CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS makes that safe to repeat. Then come two lessons in a few lines. First, the insert statement uses question marks, not f-strings. The values are passed separately, and SQLite never mixes them into the SQL text, so a customer named with a quote mark, or something worse, can never change what the statement does. That is the defence against SQL injection, and it is not optional. Second, with con. A connection used in a with block is a transaction: if the block finishes, everything in it is committed together; if anything inside raises an error, everything in it is rolled back. executemany inserts all five thousand seven hundred and ninety-seven rows in one transaction. The second with block adds a late order, then tries to insert the first row again, which breaks the primary key. The terminal shows the error, and the query below proves the rollback: the four products' lines add up to exactly five thousand seven hundred and ninety-seven, so the late order was undone too. All or nothing. But run this script a second time, and the very first insert hits every existing key. Next, making it safe to run again.

Pipelines get run twice. A scheduler retries after a failure, someone fixes a bad file and runs the job again, or a person simply presses the button twice. A good pipeline is idempotent: running it again gives the same result as running it once, never doubled data and never an error. The last section's script was not. Its second run would fail on the first primary key. This section fixes that, and protects the files as well. The folded part now holds the last section's code, records and connect. The new function load replaces October rather than adding to it. Inside one transaction, it first deletes every row dated October, then inserts the month's rows. Because both happen inside the same with block, there is no moment, even after a crash, when the table holds no October or half of it: other programs see either the old month or the new one. The function returns the row count. The terminal runs the script twice, and both runs report five thousand seven hundred and ninety-seven rows. Not double, and no error. The second danger is a crash halfway through writing a file. If the pipeline dies after writing half of the CSV, the next person to open it gets half a report, and may never know. write csv atomic avoids that. It writes everything to a temporary file next to the real one, with dot tmp added to the name, and only when that is complete does it call replace, which swaps the new file into place in a single step. On the same disk that swap is atomic: anyone reading sees the old file or the new file, never a mix. If the program dies first, the old file is untouched, and only a stray dot tmp is left.
